title: Surah Al-Kahf: Faith, Choices and Wisdom

missions.title: The Book That Guides Us

ayahs.arabic: ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ ٱلَّذِىٓ أَنزَلَ عَلَىٰ عَبْدِهِ ٱلْكِتَـٰبَ وَلَمْ يَجْعَل لَّهُۥ عِوَجَا ۜ  ﴿1﴾
ayahs.meaning: Praise belongs to Allah Who revealed the Book to His servant without crookedness.

ayahs.arabic: قَيِّمًا لِّيُنذِرَ بَأْسًا شَدِيدًا مِّن لَّدُنْهُ وَيُبَشِّرَ ٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ ٱلَّذِينَ يَعْمَلُونَ ٱلصَّـٰلِحَـٰتِ أَنَّ لَهُمْ أَجْرًا حَسَنًا  ﴿2﴾
ayahs.meaning: The Book is upright, warning of serious consequences and giving good news to believing doers of good.

ayahs.arabic: إِنَّا جَعَلْنَا مَا عَلَى ٱلْأَرْضِ زِينَةً لَّهَا لِنَبْلُوَهُمْ أَيُّهُمْ أَحْسَنُ عَمَلًا  ﴿7﴾
ayahs.meaning: What is on earth is made attractive as a test of who acts best.

ayahs.arabic: وَإِنَّا لَجَـٰعِلُونَ مَا عَلَيْهَا صَعِيدًا جُرُزًا  ﴿8﴾
ayahs.meaning: Allah can make what seems beautiful on the earth barren.

options: Ignore the promise until the game is over.
Keep your promise, then return to the game if time allows.
Tell others games are always forbidden.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-KAHF • 18:1–8  |  FOCUS: 18:1, 18:2, 18:7, 18:8  |  TRAIT: Qur’an • Purpose • Responsible choices
missions.aim: Understand why Allah revealed the Qur’an and why beautiful things in the world also test our choices.
missions.tafsir: The surah begins by praising Allah for sending a Book free of crookedness to His servant, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Its message both warns against turning away from truth and gives good news to believers who do righteous deeds. The beauty of the earth is real, yet the passage calls it a test, not a permanent trophy. Classical Tafsir explains the pairing of warning and hope: revelation guides belief and action, while worldly attraction reveals whether people choose obedience or distraction. The ending of this opening section reminds us that what looks lasting can change. For children, the lesson is not that toys, gardens or games are evil; permissible blessings can be enjoyed with gratitude. The question is whether we become so attached to them that we neglect worship, kindness and responsibility. Do not turn verses about disbelief or the Hereafter into frightening animation.
missions.story: Akhlaq was counting the bright prizes displayed at the school fair. He wanted to win every game and forgot that he had promised to help Imaan at the reading corner. When Imaan found him, she did not scold. She showed him the small children waiting for their story. “The prizes are exciting,” she said, “but our promise matters too.” Akhlaq looked at the long line. He chose to help for fifteen minutes, then enjoy the fair with his sister. That evening, Sheikh Uncle opened Surah Al-Kahf and explained that Allah lets us enjoy beautiful things while teaching us to choose what truly matters. Akhlaq smiled. His favourite memory was not the largest prize but the child who thanked him for reading.
missions.question: You want to keep playing, but you promised to help. What is the best next step?
missions.feedback: Pleasure and responsibility can fit together when we put our commitments first.
missions.action: Keep one small promise today before starting your favourite leisure activity.
missions.reflection: What good thing do I enjoy without forgetting what Allah asks of me?
missions.vocabulary: Taqwa — mindfulness of Allah; Amanah — responsibility
missions.careNote: Explain judgement and warning with hope and gentleness; do not convert verse 18:8 into catastrophic visual effects.
missions.next: Next, the Qur’an introduces young believers who made a brave choice.

missions.title: The Courageous Young Believers

ayahs.arabic: أَمْ حَسِبْتَ أَنَّ أَصْحَـٰبَ ٱلْكَهْفِ وَٱلرَّقِيمِ كَانُوا۟ مِنْ ءَايَـٰتِنَا عَجَبًا  ﴿9﴾
ayahs.meaning: The People of the Cave and the inscription are signs among Allah’s many signs.

ayahs.arabic: إِذْ أَوَى ٱلْفِتْيَةُ إِلَى ٱلْكَهْفِ فَقَالُوا۟ رَبَّنَآ ءَاتِنَا مِن لَّدُنكَ رَحْمَةً وَهَيِّئْ لَنَا مِنْ أَمْرِنَا رَشَدًا  ﴿10﴾
ayahs.meaning: The youths sought refuge in the cave and asked Allah for mercy and sound guidance.

ayahs.arabic: نَّحْنُ نَقُصُّ عَلَيْكَ نَبَأَهُم بِٱلْحَقِّ ۚ إِنَّهُمْ فِتْيَةٌ ءَامَنُوا۟ بِرَبِّهِمْ وَزِدْنَـٰهُمْ هُدًى  ﴿13﴾
ayahs.meaning: Allah tells the account truthfully: they were young people who believed, and He increased them in guidance.

ayahs.arabic: وَرَبَطْنَا عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِمْ إِذْ قَامُوا۟ فَقَالُوا۟ رَبُّنَا رَبُّ ٱلسَّمَـٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ لَن نَّدْعُوَا۟ مِن دُونِهِۦٓ إِلَـٰهًا ۖ لَّقَدْ قُلْنَآ إِذًا شَطَطًا  ﴿14﴾
ayahs.meaning: Allah strengthened their hearts as they affirmed that their Lord is Lord of the heavens and earth.

ayahs.arabic: وَإِذِ ٱعْتَزَلْتُمُوهُمْ وَمَا يَعْبُدُونَ إِلَّا ٱللَّهَ فَأْوُۥٓا۟ إِلَى ٱلْكَهْفِ يَنشُرْ لَكُمْ رَبُّكُم مِّن رَّحْمَتِهِۦ وَيُهَيِّئْ لَكُم مِّنْ أَمْرِكُم مِّرْفَقًا  ﴿16﴾
ayahs.meaning: The youths separated themselves from false worship and sought refuge in the cave, trusting Allah’s mercy.

options: Join in so nobody laughs.
Choose what is right and seek a trusted adult’s help.
Run away from home to hide.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-KAHF • 18:9–16  |  FOCUS: 18:9, 18:10, 18:13, 18:14, 18:16  |  TRAIT: Faith • Courage • Seeking wise help
missions.aim: Know that the People of the Cave were young believers who held firmly to Tawhid and asked Allah for mercy.
missions.tafsir: Verses 9–16 begin the story of the young believers, known as the People of the Cave. The Qur’an presents them as youths who believed in their Lord; Allah increased them in guidance and strengthened their hearts. They refused to worship false deities and sought a safe place when their faith was threatened. Their prayer in 18:10 asks for mercy and right guidance. Classical commentators relate their steadfastness to sincere faith and Allah’s care. The Qur’an does not require us to invent their names, exact location, or unverified conversations. Today a child is not asked to run away from home in imitation of their withdrawal to a cave. The sound application is courage to do what is right while involving safe, trustworthy adults whenever a child faces pressure, threats or danger.
missions.story: At Amanpur school, Akhlaq noticed some older students teasing a new child for refusing to join a dishonest game. Akhlaq was worried they might laugh at him too. Imaan quietly said, “Being brave is not the same as being loud.” Together they spoke to their teacher and invited the newcomer to join their reading club. Later Sheikh Uncle told them about the young believers mentioned in Surah Al-Kahf. “They trusted Allah, asked for guidance and did not surrender their faith,” he explained. “Our situations are different, but we too can choose honesty and ask for help.” Akhlaq remembered how nervous he had felt. Courage, he realized, could be as simple as making a kind choice while his hands were still trembling.
missions.question: A child is being pressured to join something dishonest. What should Imaan do?
missions.feedback: Faithful courage includes wise, safe action and seeking support.
missions.action: Ask a parent or teacher for guidance about one difficult but safe choice you are facing.
missions.reflection: How can courage be gentle as well as strong?
missions.vocabulary: Fityah — young people; Rushd — sound guidance
missions.careNote: No invented identities, dialogue or exact geography for the People of the Cave. Never encourage children to leave home.
missions.next: The story next teaches how Allah protected them in circumstances they could not control.

missions.title: Trust Without Guessing

ayahs.arabic: وَتَرَى ٱلشَّمْسَ إِذَا طَلَعَت تَّزَٰوَرُ عَن كَهْفِهِمْ ذَاتَ ٱلْيَمِينِ وَإِذَا غَرَبَت تَّقْرِضُهُمْ ذَاتَ ٱلشِّمَالِ وَهُمْ فِى فَجْوَةٍ مِّنْهُ ۚ ذَٰلِكَ مِنْ ءَايَـٰتِ ٱللَّهِ ۗ مَن يَهْدِ ٱللَّهُ فَهُوَ ٱلْمُهْتَدِ ۖ وَمَن يُضْلِلْ فَلَن تَجِدَ لَهُۥ وَلِيًّا مُّرْشِدًا  ﴿17﴾
ayahs.meaning: Allah describes how the sun’s light passed by the cave as part of His care.

ayahs.arabic: وَتَحْسَبُهُمْ أَيْقَاظًا وَهُمْ رُقُودٌ ۚ وَنُقَلِّبُهُمْ ذَاتَ ٱلْيَمِينِ وَذَاتَ ٱلشِّمَالِ ۖ وَكَلْبُهُم بَـٰسِطٌ ذِرَاعَيْهِ بِٱلْوَصِيدِ ۚ لَوِ ٱطَّلَعْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ لَوَلَّيْتَ مِنْهُمْ فِرَارًا وَلَمُلِئْتَ مِنْهُمْ رُعْبًا  ﴿18﴾
ayahs.meaning: The youths appeared awake though asleep; Allah turned them from side to side, and their dog lay at the entrance.

ayahs.arabic: وَكَذَٰلِكَ بَعَثْنَـٰهُمْ لِيَتَسَآءَلُوا۟ بَيْنَهُمْ ۚ قَالَ قَآئِلٌ مِّنْهُمْ كَمْ لَبِثْتُمْ ۖ قَالُوا۟ لَبِثْنَا يَوْمًا أَوْ بَعْضَ يَوْمٍ ۚ قَالُوا۟ رَبُّكُمْ أَعْلَمُ بِمَا لَبِثْتُمْ فَٱبْعَثُوٓا۟ أَحَدَكُم بِوَرِقِكُمْ هَـٰذِهِۦٓ إِلَى ٱلْمَدِينَةِ فَلْيَنظُرْ أَيُّهَآ أَزْكَىٰ طَعَامًا فَلْيَأْتِكُم بِرِزْقٍ مِّنْهُ وَلْيَتَلَطَّفْ وَلَا يُشْعِرَنَّ بِكُمْ أَحَدًا  ﴿19﴾
ayahs.meaning: Allah awakened the youths; they wondered how long they had stayed and sent someone carefully to buy food.

ayahs.arabic: وَكَذَٰلِكَ أَعْثَرْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ لِيَعْلَمُوٓا۟ أَنَّ وَعْدَ ٱللَّهِ حَقٌّ وَأَنَّ ٱلسَّاعَةَ لَا رَيْبَ فِيهَآ إِذْ يَتَنَـٰزَعُونَ بَيْنَهُمْ أَمْرَهُمْ ۖ فَقَالُوا۟ ٱبْنُوا۟ عَلَيْهِم بُنْيَـٰنًا ۖ رَّبُّهُمْ أَعْلَمُ بِهِمْ ۚ قَالَ ٱلَّذِينَ غَلَبُوا۟ عَلَىٰٓ أَمْرِهِمْ لَنَتَّخِذَنَّ عَلَيْهِم مَّسْجِدًا  ﴿21﴾
ayahs.meaning: Their story helped people understand that Allah’s promise and the Hour are true.

ayahs.arabic: سَيَقُولُونَ ثَلَـٰثَةٌ رَّابِعُهُمْ كَلْبُهُمْ وَيَقُولُونَ خَمْسَةٌ سَادِسُهُمْ كَلْبُهُمْ رَجْمًۢا بِٱلْغَيْبِ ۖ وَيَقُولُونَ سَبْعَةٌ وَثَامِنُهُمْ كَلْبُهُمْ ۚ قُل رَّبِّىٓ أَعْلَمُ بِعِدَّتِهِم مَّا يَعْلَمُهُمْ إِلَّا قَلِيلٌ ۗ فَلَا تُمَارِ فِيهِمْ إِلَّا مِرَآءً ظَـٰهِرًا وَلَا تَسْتَفْتِ فِيهِم مِّنْهُمْ أَحَدًا  ﴿22﴾
ayahs.meaning: People disputed their number; Allah knows best, and pointless arguments should be avoided.

options: Insist on your favourite guess.
State what is known and admit what is uncertain.
Invent a new detail to end the debate.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-KAHF • 18:17–22  |  FOCUS: 18:17, 18:18, 18:19, 18:21, 18:22  |  TRAIT: Trust • Humility • Limits of knowledge
missions.aim: Learn to respect what Allah has revealed and avoid confident guesses about the unseen.
missions.tafsir: Allah describes the unusual protection of the People of the Cave, their awakening after a long period, and their careful exchange about food and safety. The account points to Allah’s power and the truth of resurrection. Verse 22 explains that people disagreed over the youths’ number. Allah directs His Messenger ﷺ away from fruitless speculation, because the exact number is not the central lesson. Classical Tafsir discusses reports on these details but keeps revelation authoritative over conjecture. The narrative calls children to wonder at Allah’s signs while distinguishing knowledge from guesses. The dog and the cave are in the Qur’an; unverified names or fanciful magical powers are not. Children should not be assessed on disputed numbers of the youths or animals; the learning target is truthfulness about what is known.
missions.story: Akhlaq discovered an old photograph of Amanpur’s first library. He announced that it had been built exactly one hundred years ago. Dadi Jaan asked how he knew. “I guessed,” he admitted. Imaan suggested they ask the librarian. They learned the building was younger than he imagined. Instead of feeling embarrassed, Akhlaq wrote “We are still checking” beneath their school display. Sheikh Uncle then reminded them that the Qur’an does not encourage endless argument about the number of the People of the Cave. “You can be curious,” he said, “and still say, ‘Allah knows best,’ when you do not have proof.” Akhlaq discovered that an honest question was more useful than a confident guess.
missions.question: Friends disagree about a detail the Qur’an does not clearly settle. What is wise?
missions.feedback: Truthfulness includes knowing the limits of your knowledge.
missions.action: Say “I am not sure; let me check” once when you do not know an answer.
missions.reflection: Which is stronger: pretending certainty or asking carefully?
missions.careNote: Avoid turning disputed counts, names, time periods or locations into memorization facts. Do not animate people’s faces as historically verified.
missions.next: Now the Qur’an teaches how to speak responsibly about tomorrow.

missions.title: Tomorrow, In Sha Allah

ayahs.arabic: وَلَا تَقُولَنَّ لِشَا۟ىْءٍ إِنِّى فَاعِلٌ ذَٰلِكَ غَدًا  ﴿23﴾
ayahs.meaning: Do not confidently promise to do something tomorrow as though you control the future.

ayahs.arabic: إِلَّآ أَن يَشَآءَ ٱللَّهُ ۚ وَٱذْكُر رَّبَّكَ إِذَا نَسِيتَ وَقُلْ عَسَىٰٓ أَن يَهْدِيَنِ رَبِّى لِأَقْرَبَ مِنْ هَـٰذَا رَشَدًا  ﴿24﴾
ayahs.meaning: Say “if Allah wills,” remember your Lord when you forget, and seek better guidance.

ayahs.arabic: وَلَبِثُوا۟ فِى كَهْفِهِمْ ثَلَـٰثَ مِا۟ئَةٍ سِنِينَ وَٱزْدَادُوا۟ تِسْعًا  ﴿25﴾
ayahs.meaning: The passage states the long period the youths remained in the cave.

ayahs.arabic: قُلِ ٱللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ بِمَا لَبِثُوا۟ ۖ لَهُۥ غَيْبُ ٱلسَّمَـٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ ۖ أَبْصِرْ بِهِۦ وَأَسْمِعْ ۚ مَا لَهُم مِّن دُونِهِۦ مِن وَلِىٍّ وَلَا يُشْرِكُ فِى حُكْمِهِۦٓ أَحَدًا  ﴿26﴾
ayahs.meaning: Allah knows best how long they remained and possesses the unseen of the heavens and earth.

options: Say he controls every result.
Say “In sha Allah,” make a realistic plan, and work on it.
Say “In sha Allah” but make no effort.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-KAHF • 18:23–26  |  FOCUS: 18:23, 18:24, 18:25, 18:26  |  TRAIT: Humility • Planning • Reliance on Allah
missions.aim: Practise saying “In sha Allah” sincerely while still preparing and keeping promises.
missions.tafsir: Verses 23–24 teach believers not to speak of a future undertaking as if they control tomorrow. Instead, we acknowledge the will of Allah and remember Him if we forget. Verses 25–26 return to the duration of the stay and Allah’s complete knowledge of the unseen. Tafsir connects these teachings to humility before divine knowledge, not to abandoning effort. “In sha Allah” is not an excuse for intentionally breaking promises. We can plan carefully, seek help and do our best while admitting that outcomes rest with Allah. The numbers mentioned in 18:25 are part of the revealed wording; do not turn speculative chronological theories into doctrinal quiz questions. For young children, the practical learning is to make realistic plans and speak humbly about future events.
missions.story: Akhlaq told everyone he would finish a large science model overnight. Salaam asked whether he had the materials. “Not yet,” Akhlaq replied, “but I’ll definitely finish!” Imaan helped him list the supplies and divide the work into smaller steps. “In sha Allah, we’ll finish the first part tomorrow,” she said. When rain delayed their visit to the shop, they adjusted the plan instead of blaming one another. Sheikh Uncle explained that believers plan responsibly while remembering that Allah knows what tomorrow brings. Akhlaq learned to say “In sha Allah” with sincerity, not as a way to escape his work. His model improved because he paired reliance on Allah with effort.
missions.question: How should Akhlaq speak about tomorrow’s project?
missions.feedback: Relying on Allah goes with honest preparation and responsible action.
missions.action: Make one realistic plan for tomorrow and add “In sha Allah” when speaking about it.
missions.reflection: What part of my plans can I control, and what belongs to Allah?
missions.vocabulary: In sha Allah — if Allah wills; Tawakkul — reliance on Allah
missions.careNote: Never imply invoking the phrase guarantees success; avoid weaponizing it as permission to break promises.
missions.next: Having trusted Allah, the surah turns to whose friendship and approval matter.

missions.title: Good Friends, Real Treasure

ayahs.arabic: وَٱتْلُ مَآ أُوحِىَ إِلَيْكَ مِن كِتَابِ رَبِّكَ ۖ لَا مُبَدِّلَ لِكَلِمَـٰتِهِۦ وَلَن تَجِدَ مِن دُونِهِۦ مُلْتَحَدًا  ﴿27﴾
ayahs.meaning: Recite what has been revealed; none can change Allah’s words.

ayahs.arabic: وَٱصْبِرْ نَفْسَكَ مَعَ ٱلَّذِينَ يَدْعُونَ رَبَّهُم بِٱلْغَدَوٰةِ وَٱلْعَشِىِّ يُرِيدُونَ وَجْهَهُۥ ۖ وَلَا تَعْدُ عَيْنَاكَ عَنْهُمْ تُرِيدُ زِينَةَ ٱلْحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا ۖ وَلَا تُطِعْ مَنْ أَغْفَلْنَا قَلْبَهُۥ عَن ذِكْرِنَا وَٱتَّبَعَ هَوَىٰهُ وَكَانَ أَمْرُهُۥ فُرُطًا  ﴿28﴾
ayahs.meaning: Be patient with those who call upon their Lord sincerely; do not chase mere worldly display.

ayahs.arabic: وَقُلِ ٱلْحَقُّ مِن رَّبِّكُمْ ۖ فَمَن شَآءَ فَلْيُؤْمِن وَمَن شَآءَ فَلْيَكْفُرْ ۚ إِنَّآ أَعْتَدْنَا لِلظَّـٰلِمِينَ نَارًا أَحَاطَ بِهِمْ سُرَادِقُهَا ۚ وَإِن يَسْتَغِيثُوا۟ يُغَاثُوا۟ بِمَآءٍ كَٱلْمُهْلِ يَشْوِى ٱلْوُجُوهَ ۚ بِئْسَ ٱلشَّرَابُ وَسَآءَتْ مُرْتَفَقًا  ﴿29﴾
ayahs.meaning: Truth is from the Lord, and people are accountable for how they respond.

ayahs.arabic: إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ وَعَمِلُوا۟ ٱلصَّـٰلِحَـٰتِ إِنَّا لَا نُضِيعُ أَجْرَ مَنْ أَحْسَنَ عَمَلًا  ﴿30﴾
ayahs.meaning: Allah does not allow the reward of sincere righteous action to be lost.

ayahs.arabic: أُو۟لَـٰٓئِكَ لَهُمْ جَنَّـٰتُ عَدْنٍ تَجْرِى مِن تَحْتِهِمُ ٱلْأَنْهَـٰرُ يُحَلَّوْنَ فِيهَا مِنْ أَسَاوِرَ مِن ذَهَبٍ وَيَلْبَسُونَ ثِيَابًا خُضْرًا مِّن سُندُسٍ وَإِسْتَبْرَقٍ مُّتَّكِـِٔينَ فِيهَا عَلَى ٱلْأَرَآئِكِ ۚ نِعْمَ ٱلثَّوَابُ وَحَسُنَتْ مُرْتَفَقًا  ﴿31﴾
ayahs.meaning: The passage describes the good reward of believing people who do right.

options: Only classmates with expensive devices.
People who treat others respectfully and want to learn.
Only the loudest speakers.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-KAHF • 18:27–31  |  FOCUS: 18:27, 18:28, 18:29, 18:30, 18:31  |  TRAIT: Friendship • Worship • Dignity
missions.aim: Value sincere faith and good company over popularity or expensive possessions.
missions.tafsir: The Prophet ﷺ is instructed to recite revelation faithfully and to remain patiently with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His pleasure. The verses caution against being captivated by outward adornment and following the desires of heedless people. They then contrast the consequences of turning from faith with the reward promised to righteous believers. Classical commentators stress the worth of the devoted believers even when society regards them as poor or unimportant. For children, this is not a ranking of classmates’ wealth or a reason to withdraw from every child who thinks differently. The important habit is choosing friendships that strengthen honesty, worship and kindness, while treating everyone with dignity. Descriptions of the Hereafter should be conveyed faithfully and without frightening gameplay.
missions.story: Akhlaq’s class planned a reading group. One group insisted that children with the newest tablets should lead. Mohsin, whose tablet was old, quietly walked away. Imaan invited him back. “He has the best story ideas,” she said. They decided everyone could contribute something different: a notebook, a question, a drawing or a clear reading voice. At home Sheikh Uncle explained the Qur’anic instruction to value sincere company rather than dazzling appearances. Akhlaq realized he had sometimes chosen friends by their possessions without noticing how they treated others. The next day he sat beside Mohsin and listened to his thoughtful question. Their new friendship began with a simple act of respect.
missions.question: Who should be welcomed into the reading group?
missions.feedback: Good company is measured by sincere character, not social status.
missions.action: Invite someone who is often left out to join one safe group activity.
missions.reflection: What makes someone a genuinely good companion?
missions.careNote: Avoid exclusion of non-Muslim peers, poverty shaming or using Paradise images as prize tokens.
missions.next: Next comes a story about a person who mistook wealth for permanent greatness.
missions.sourcePath: Qur’an 18:27–31 • al-Tabari / Ibn Kathir / al-Munir • https://quran.com/18/27

missions.title: The Proud Garden Owner

ayahs.arabic: وَٱضْرِبْ لَهُم مَّثَلًا رَّجُلَيْنِ جَعَلْنَا لِأَحَدِهِمَا جَنَّتَيْنِ مِنْ أَعْنَـٰبٍ وَحَفَفْنَـٰهُمَا بِنَخْلٍ وَجَعَلْنَا بَيْنَهُمَا زَرْعًا  ﴿32﴾
ayahs.meaning: Allah gives an example of two men, one granted flourishing gardens.

ayahs.arabic: كِلْتَا ٱلْجَنَّتَيْنِ ءَاتَتْ أُكُلَهَا وَلَمْ تَظْلِم مِّنْهُ شَيْـًٔا ۚ وَفَجَّرْنَا خِلَـٰلَهُمَا نَهَرًا  ﴿33﴾
ayahs.meaning: The two gardens produced fruit, and water flowed through them.

ayahs.arabic: وَكَانَ لَهُۥ ثَمَرٌ فَقَالَ لِصَـٰحِبِهِۦ وَهُوَ يُحَاوِرُهُۥٓ أَنَا۠ أَكْثَرُ مِنكَ مَالًا وَأَعَزُّ نَفَرًا  ﴿34﴾
ayahs.meaning: The garden owner boasted that he had more wealth and stronger support.

ayahs.arabic: وَدَخَلَ جَنَّتَهُۥ وَهُوَ ظَالِمٌ لِّنَفْسِهِۦ قَالَ مَآ أَظُنُّ أَن تَبِيدَ هَـٰذِهِۦٓ أَبَدًا  ﴿35﴾
ayahs.meaning: He entered his garden wronging himself and imagined it would never perish.

ayahs.arabic: وَمَآ أَظُنُّ ٱلسَّاعَةَ قَآئِمَةً وَلَئِن رُّدِدتُّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّى لَأَجِدَنَّ خَيْرًا مِّنْهَا مُنقَلَبًا  ﴿36﴾
ayahs.meaning: He doubted the Hour and assumed he would receive even better if returned to his Lord.

options: Boast that nobody has anything as good.
Thank Allah and share joy without looking down on others.
Hide it forever because having gifts is wrong.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-KAHF • 18:32–36  |  FOCUS: 18:32, 18:33, 18:34, 18:35, 18:36  |  TRAIT: Gratitude • Humility • Respect
missions.aim: Notice the danger of boasting about wealth and imagining that blessings can never change.
missions.tafsir: Allah gives the example of two men, one granted fertile gardens, crops and water. The wealthy owner boasts about his riches and social strength. He enters his garden while wronging himself and claims that it will never perish, even speaking arrogantly about the Last Day. Classical Tafsir presents the garden as a test of belief and gratitude, not as evidence that wealth itself is sinful. The owner’s failure is his pride and false security. Children should understand that having nice things does not make someone bad, nor does having fewer things make someone inferior. What matters is how blessings are used, whether Allah is thanked, and whether others are treated with dignity. The garden becomes a gentle mirror for attitudes about possessions, praise and comparisons.
missions.story: Seith Javed donated beautiful plants to the Amanpur school garden. Akhlaq was impressed by the rarest plant and told everyone that their school now had “the best garden in the city.” When a younger child arrived carrying a tiny seedling in a recycled pot, Akhlaq nearly laughed at its size. Imaan said, “That seedling matters too.” They planted it in a sunny corner. Later Sheikh Uncle narrated the Qur’anic example of a wealthy garden owner whose pride made him forget the Giver of blessings. Akhlaq looked at the plants differently. Every leaf needed water, care and Allah’s permission to grow. The smallest plant deserved attention, and the children who cared for it deserved respect.
missions.question: Akhlaq has a new expensive gift. What is the best way to respond?
missions.feedback: Blessings call for gratitude, not arrogance or shame.
missions.action: Thank Allah for one blessing and share it kindly without showing off.
missions.reflection: How can a blessing become a test of our character?
missions.careNote: No assumption that rich people are wicked. Maintain the original belief in resurrection.
missions.next: The second man now responds, and the garden story moves toward its lesson.
missions.sourcePath: Qur’an 18:32–36 • al-Tabari / Ibn Kathir / al-Munir • https://quran.com/18/32

missions.title: Remember the Giver

ayahs.arabic: قَالَ لَهُۥ صَاحِبُهُۥ وَهُوَ يُحَاوِرُهُۥٓ أَكَفَرْتَ بِٱلَّذِى خَلَقَكَ مِن تُرَابٍ ثُمَّ مِن نُّطْفَةٍ ثُمَّ سَوَّىٰكَ رَجُلًا  ﴿37﴾
ayahs.meaning: His companion reminded him of Allah who created and formed him.

ayahs.arabic: لَّـٰكِنَّا۠ هُوَ ٱللَّهُ رَبِّى وَلَآ أُشْرِكُ بِرَبِّىٓ أَحَدًا  ﴿38﴾
ayahs.meaning: The believing companion affirmed Allah as his Lord and refused to associate partners with Him.

ayahs.arabic: وَلَوْلَآ إِذْ دَخَلْتَ جَنَّتَكَ قُلْتَ مَا شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ لَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِٱللَّهِ ۚ إِن تَرَنِ أَنَا۠ أَقَلَّ مِنكَ مَالًا وَوَلَدًا  ﴿39﴾
ayahs.meaning: He advised acknowledging Allah’s will and power when entering the garden.

ayahs.arabic: فَعَسَىٰ رَبِّىٓ أَن يُؤْتِيَنِ خَيْرًا مِّن جَنَّتِكَ وَيُرْسِلَ عَلَيْهَا حُسْبَانًا مِّنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ فَتُصْبِحَ صَعِيدًا زَلَقًا  ﴿40﴾
ayahs.meaning: The companion reminded him that Allah could grant something better or allow the garden to be lost.

ayahs.arabic: وَأُحِيطَ بِثَمَرِهِۦ فَأَصْبَحَ يُقَلِّبُ كَفَّيْهِ عَلَىٰ مَآ أَنفَقَ فِيهَا وَهِىَ خَاوِيَةٌ عَلَىٰ عُرُوشِهَا وَيَقُولُ يَـٰلَيْتَنِى لَمْ أُشْرِكْ بِرَبِّىٓ أَحَدًا  ﴿42﴾
ayahs.meaning: The garden was ruined; its owner regretted his pride and association of partners with Allah.

ayahs.arabic: هُنَالِكَ ٱلْوَلَـٰيَةُ لِلَّهِ ٱلْحَقِّ ۚ هُوَ خَيْرٌ ثَوَابًا وَخَيْرٌ عُقْبًا  ﴿44﴾
ayahs.meaning: All true authority and help belong to Allah.

options: “Only I could ever achieve this.”
“Mā shāʾ Allah; lā quwwata illā billāh,” with sincere gratitude.
“People with less do not matter.”
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-KAHF • 18:37–44  |  FOCUS: 18:37, 18:38, 18:39, 18:40, 18:42, 18:44  |  TRAIT: Gratitude • Wise counsel • Resilience
missions.aim: Learn a Qur’anic way of responding to blessings and practise giving advice without humiliation.
missions.tafsir: The believing companion reminds the garden owner that Allah created and sustains him. He speaks of belief in the one Lord and teaches the owner to recognise Allah’s will and power when admiring his property: “Mā shāʾ Allah; lā quwwata illā billāh.” The passage then describes the loss of the gardens and the owner’s regret. Classical Tafsir highlights the contrast between prideful confidence in possessions and humility before Allah. The text does not say we can predict the financial future of a particular person from their character. For children, the teaching is to receive advice respectfully, be thankful for blessings and respond to setbacks without mocking someone who has suffered. The story ends by affirming that true protection and authority belong to Allah.
missions.story: After the school garden survived a storm, Akhlaq proudly said, “I saved everything myself!” Imaan reminded him how Mohsina had covered the seedlings and how the gardener had secured the gate. Sheikh Uncle told them about the believing companion in the garden story who redirected pride toward gratitude. “You can be happy about your hard work,” he said, “and still thank Allah and everyone who helped.” Akhlaq invited his classmates to inspect the plants and thanked them by name. When they discovered one damaged pot, he did not blame anyone. They replanted it together. His happiness felt steadier because it was not built on claiming every success for himself.
missions.question: What should a child say when admiring a beautiful blessing?
missions.feedback: The Qur’an teaches us to recognise Allah’s will and power while using our abilities responsibly.
missions.action: Say “Mā shāʾ Allah; lā quwwata illā billāh” when admiring one blessing, and thank someone who helped.
missions.reflection: How does gratitude change how I respond to success?
missions.vocabulary: Mā shāʾ Allah — what Allah wills; Quwwah — strength
missions.careNote: Do not promise that a phrase automatically protects a possession from all damage. No disaster-based punishment game.
missions.next: The surah then widens our view: what can last when worldly things change?
missions.sourcePath: Qur’an 18:37–44 • al-Tabari / Ibn Kathir / al-Munir • https://quran.com/18/37

missions.title: What Lasts Beyond the World

ayahs.arabic: وَٱضْرِبْ لَهُم مَّثَلَ ٱلْحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا كَمَآءٍ أَنزَلْنَـٰهُ مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ فَٱخْتَلَطَ بِهِۦ نَبَاتُ ٱلْأَرْضِ فَأَصْبَحَ هَشِيمًا تَذْرُوهُ ٱلرِّيَـٰحُ ۗ وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَىْءٍ مُّقْتَدِرًا  ﴿45﴾
ayahs.meaning: Worldly life is compared to vegetation that flourishes after rain and then becomes scattered.

ayahs.arabic: ٱلْمَالُ وَٱلْبَنُونَ زِينَةُ ٱلْحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا ۖ وَٱلْبَـٰقِيَـٰتُ ٱلصَّـٰلِحَـٰتُ خَيْرٌ عِندَ رَبِّكَ ثَوَابًا وَخَيْرٌ أَمَلًا  ﴿46﴾
ayahs.meaning: Wealth and children are adornments of life, while lasting righteous deeds are better with Allah.

ayahs.arabic: وَوُضِعَ ٱلْكِتَـٰبُ فَتَرَى ٱلْمُجْرِمِينَ مُشْفِقِينَ مِمَّا فِيهِ وَيَقُولُونَ يَـٰوَيْلَتَنَا مَالِ هَـٰذَا ٱلْكِتَـٰبِ لَا يُغَادِرُ صَغِيرَةً وَلَا كَبِيرَةً إِلَّآ أَحْصَىٰهَا ۚ وَوَجَدُوا۟ مَا عَمِلُوا۟ حَاضِرًا ۗ وَلَا يَظْلِمُ رَبُّكَ أَحَدًا  ﴿49﴾
ayahs.meaning: The record of deeds is presented; no injustice is done by Allah.

ayahs.arabic: وَإِذْ قُلْنَا لِلْمَلَـٰٓئِكَةِ ٱسْجُدُوا۟ لِـَٔادَمَ فَسَجَدُوٓا۟ إِلَّآ إِبْلِيسَ كَانَ مِنَ ٱلْجِنِّ فَفَسَقَ عَنْ أَمْرِ رَبِّهِۦٓ ۗ أَفَتَتَّخِذُونَهُۥ وَذُرِّيَّتَهُۥٓ أَوْلِيَآءَ مِن دُونِى وَهُمْ لَكُمْ عَدُوٌّۢ ۚ بِئْسَ لِلظَّـٰلِمِينَ بَدَلًا  ﴿50﴾
ayahs.meaning: Iblis was of the jinn and rebelled against his Lord’s command.

ayahs.arabic: وَلَقَدْ صَرَّفْنَا فِى هَـٰذَا ٱلْقُرْءَانِ لِلنَّاسِ مِن كُلِّ مَثَلٍ ۚ وَكَانَ ٱلْإِنسَـٰنُ أَكْثَرَ شَىْءٍ جَدَلًا  ﴿54﴾
ayahs.meaning: The Qur’an contains varied explanations and examples, though people often dispute.

ayahs.arabic: وَرَبُّكَ ٱلْغَفُورُ ذُو ٱلرَّحْمَةِ ۖ لَوْ يُؤَاخِذُهُم بِمَا كَسَبُوا۟ لَعَجَّلَ لَهُمُ ٱلْعَذَابَ ۚ بَل لَّهُم مَّوْعِدٌ لَّن يَجِدُوا۟ مِن دُونِهِۦ مَوْئِلًا  ﴿58﴾
ayahs.meaning: Allah is Forgiving and Merciful, yet accountability occurs at an appointed time.

options: Show off a toy to make others jealous.
Help a younger student learn something useful.
Keep every useful thing only for yourself.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-KAHF • 18:45–59  |  FOCUS: 18:45, 18:46, 18:49, 18:50, 18:54, 18:58  |  TRAIT: Good deeds • Accountability • Mercy
missions.aim: Recognize that good deeds outlast possessions and that Allah calls us to reflect, repent and act responsibly.
missions.tafsir: The Qur’an compares worldly life to vegetation that grows after rain and then dries and scatters. Wealth and children are described as adornments, while lasting righteous deeds are better in reward and hope. Later verses speak of the record of deeds, the danger of taking Iblis and his allies as guides, varied Qur’anic examples, and Allah’s mercy and appointed timing. These are substantial theological passages, not merely slogans about tidying rooms. Classical scholars describe the temporary nature of worldly adornment and the reality of accountability before Allah. Child-facing teaching should combine seriousness with hope: mistakes can be acknowledged and repented of, and good deeds matter even when unnoticed. Never turn divine judgement into an app meter or use fearful imagery to pressure children into checking boxes.
missions.story: Dadi Jaan found an old box of photographs while Imaan and Akhlaq were cleaning the family cupboard. Some showed toys that had broken years ago; others showed meals shared with neighbours and days spent helping at school. Akhlaq was surprised by which memories made everyone smile. “The toy was fun,” said Salaam, “but your kindness left a longer mark.” They discussed how the Qur’an calls worldly things beautiful yet temporary and reminds people of lasting good deeds. That evening Akhlaq decided to help sort the family books for younger children. He did not receive a prize. Instead, he watched a small boy choose a book with delight and understood why good actions are worth repeating.
missions.question: Which choice is most likely to leave a lasting good effect?
missions.feedback: Righteous action matters beyond applause or possessions.
missions.action: Help someone with one useful task today without asking for a reward.
missions.reflection: What good deed could benefit someone after I have forgotten doing it?
missions.vocabulary: Bāqiyāt ṣāliḥāt — lasting righteous deeds; Rahmah — mercy
missions.careNote: Handle Judgement, Iblis and Hell with text-grounded age gating; never portray divine knowledge as surveillance mechanics.
missions.next: We now follow Prophet Musa (AS) as he travels in pursuit of knowledge.
missions.sourcePath: Qur’an 18:45–59 • al-Tabari / Ibn Kathir / al-Munir • https://quran.com/18/45

missions.title: A Journey for Knowledge

ayahs.arabic: وَإِذْ قَالَ مُوسَىٰ لِفَتَىٰهُ لَآ أَبْرَحُ حَتَّىٰٓ أَبْلُغَ مَجْمَعَ ٱلْبَحْرَيْنِ أَوْ أَمْضِىَ حُقُبًا  ﴿60﴾
ayahs.meaning: Musa said he would keep travelling until reaching the meeting of two seas, however long it took.

ayahs.arabic: فَلَمَّا جَاوَزَا قَالَ لِفَتَىٰهُ ءَاتِنَا غَدَآءَنَا لَقَدْ لَقِينَا مِن سَفَرِنَا هَـٰذَا نَصَبًا  ﴿62﴾
ayahs.meaning: Musa asked for food after the travellers had passed their destination.

ayahs.arabic: فَوَجَدَا عَبْدًا مِّنْ عِبَادِنَآ ءَاتَيْنَـٰهُ رَحْمَةً مِّنْ عِندِنَا وَعَلَّمْنَـٰهُ مِن لَّدُنَّا عِلْمًا  ﴿65﴾
ayahs.meaning: They found a servant given mercy and particular knowledge from Allah.

options: Pretend you already know.
Ask a trustworthy teacher and keep learning.
Mock the person who explains slowly.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-KAHF • 18:60–65  |  FOCUS: 18:60, 18:62, 18:65  |  TRAIT: Curiosity • Perseverance • Humility
missions.aim: Admire Prophet Musa’s (AS) determination to seek knowledge and the value of learning from others.
missions.tafsir: Surah Al-Kahf recounts that Prophet Musa (AS) travelled with his young companion to seek a servant of Allah who had received special mercy and knowledge. Their journey was not simply sightseeing; it involved purpose, persistence and a willingness to learn. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir discuss the account and the identity of the companion in narrated reports. The Qur’an itself presents learning as something worthy of effort and humility. A child may discover that even a knowledgeable person seeks further understanding. This does not mean every adult who claims secret knowledge should be believed. The story concerns Allah’s special instruction, not ordinary excuses for ignoring evidence or safety. In the app, depict footsteps, a shoreline and study tools; do not create facial portrayals or fictional dialogue attributed to Musa (AS).
missions.story: Imaan wanted to learn how to care for the school’s drinking-water filter. She assumed it was too complicated. The caretaker offered to demonstrate, but she hesitated to ask questions. Akhlaq reminded her of the story of Musa (AS) travelling to learn. “If a Prophet could seek knowledge,” he said, “we can certainly ask a kind question.” Imaan watched the demonstration carefully and discovered why cleaning the filter mattered. Then she drew a simple instruction sheet for younger classmates. She felt proud, not because she knew everything, but because she had learned something useful and shared it respectfully.
missions.question: You do not understand an important lesson. What should you do?
missions.feedback: Curiosity and humility help us learn safely.
missions.action: Ask one thoughtful question about something useful you want to understand.
missions.reflection: Who taught me something valuable this week?
missions.careNote: No invented geographical certainty or depictions of Musa (AS); distinguish divinely granted knowledge from ordinary secret claims.
missions.next: The next scene teaches that learning sometimes requires patience when answers are incomplete.
missions.sourcePath: Qur’an 18:60–65 • al-Tabari / Ibn Kathir / al-Munir • https://quran.com/18/60

missions.title: A Promise of Patience

ayahs.arabic: قَالَ لَهُۥ مُوسَىٰ هَلْ أَتَّبِعُكَ عَلَىٰٓ أَن تُعَلِّمَنِ مِمَّا عُلِّمْتَ رُشْدًا  ﴿66﴾
ayahs.meaning: Musa respectfully asked to follow and learn the guidance the servant had been taught.

ayahs.arabic: قَالَ إِنَّكَ لَن تَسْتَطِيعَ مَعِىَ صَبْرًا  ﴿67﴾
ayahs.meaning: The servant warned Musa that patience would be difficult.

ayahs.arabic: وَكَيْفَ تَصْبِرُ عَلَىٰ مَا لَمْ تُحِطْ بِهِۦ خُبْرًا  ﴿68﴾
ayahs.meaning: How could Musa be patient regarding something he did not fully understand?

ayahs.arabic: قَالَ سَتَجِدُنِىٓ إِن شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ صَابِرًا وَلَآ أَعْصِى لَكَ أَمْرًا  ﴿69﴾
ayahs.meaning: Musa expressed his intention to be patient, if Allah willed.

ayahs.arabic: قَالَ فَإِنِ ٱتَّبَعْتَنِى فَلَا تَسْـَٔلْنِى عَن شَىْءٍ حَتَّىٰٓ أُحْدِثَ لَكَ مِنْهُ ذِكْرًا  ﴿70﴾
ayahs.meaning: The servant asked Musa not to question events until an explanation was given.

options: Interrupt at every second.
Listen carefully and ask a respectful question at the right moment.
Never ask adults questions, even when unsafe.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-KAHF • 18:66–70  |  FOCUS: 18:66, 18:67, 18:68, 18:69, 18:70  |  TRAIT: Patience • Respectful questions • Learning limits
missions.aim: Understand that patience can help us learn, but respectful questions and personal safety still matter.
missions.tafsir: Musa (AS) respectfully asks whether he may follow the specially taught servant and learn right guidance. The servant explains that Musa will find it difficult to remain patient about matters he cannot yet understand. Musa intends, by Allah’s will, to be patient, and a condition about asking questions until explanations are offered is stated. Classical Tafsir treats this conversation within its specific sacred narrative; it is not a universal order that children must obey any adult without questions. Children should be allowed to ask for clarification, challenge wrongdoing safely and tell trusted adults about worrying situations. The lesson is distinguishing impatience from thoughtful inquiry: sometimes we need to listen longer before understanding a harmless activity, while genuine danger calls for immediate help.
missions.story: During an art class, the teacher asked the children to fold paper in a strange way before drawing. Akhlaq wanted to interrupt, but Imaan suggested watching the first two steps. When the folds opened into a beautiful geometric pattern, he understood the reason. After class, he asked the teacher how the pattern worked, and she happily explained. Sheikh Uncle later connected their experience to the patience shown in Musa’s (AS) journey. “Waiting can help us learn,” he said, “but you must always speak up when something feels unsafe or wrong.” Akhlaq decided that patience meant paying attention, not hiding genuine concerns.
missions.question: An unfamiliar but safe activity is being explained. What is a good first response?
missions.feedback: Patience supports learning; it does not cancel a child’s right to seek safety.
missions.action: During one safe lesson today, listen until the explanation finishes before asking your question.
missions.reflection: When did patience help me understand something better?
missions.careNote: Prominently state safeguarding override: children must report harm and can refuse unsafe instructions.
missions.next: An unusual sequence follows, requiring particularly careful adult-led explanation.
missions.sourcePath: Qur’an 18:66–70 • al-Tabari / Ibn Kathir / al-Munir • https://quran.com/18/66

missions.title: When the Story Becomes Difficult

ayahs.arabic: فَٱنطَلَقَا حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَا رَكِبَا فِى ٱلسَّفِينَةِ خَرَقَهَا ۖ قَالَ أَخَرَقْتَهَا لِتُغْرِقَ أَهْلَهَا لَقَدْ جِئْتَ شَيْـًٔا إِمْرًا  ﴿71﴾
ayahs.meaning: They boarded a boat; the servant made a hole, which Musa questioned as a dangerous action.

ayahs.arabic: فَٱنطَلَقَا حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَا لَقِيَا غُلَـٰمًا فَقَتَلَهُۥ قَالَ أَقَتَلْتَ نَفْسًا زَكِيَّةًۢ بِغَيْرِ نَفْسٍ لَّقَدْ جِئْتَ شَيْـًٔا نُّكْرًا  ﴿74﴾
ayahs.meaning: The narrative records a tragic death, which Musa strongly questioned.

ayahs.arabic: فَٱنطَلَقَا حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَآ أَتَيَآ أَهْلَ قَرْيَةٍ ٱسْتَطْعَمَآ أَهْلَهَا فَأَبَوْا۟ أَن يُضَيِّفُوهُمَا فَوَجَدَا فِيهَا جِدَارًا يُرِيدُ أَن يَنقَضَّ فَأَقَامَهُۥ ۖ قَالَ لَوْ شِئْتَ لَتَّخَذْتَ عَلَيْهِ أَجْرًا  ﴿77﴾
ayahs.meaning: They reached a town whose people declined hospitality; the servant repaired a falling wall.

ayahs.arabic: قَالَ هَـٰذَا فِرَاقُ بَيْنِى وَبَيْنِكَ ۚ سَأُنَبِّئُكَ بِتَأْوِيلِ مَا لَمْ تَسْتَطِع عَّلَيْهِ صَبْرًا  ﴿78﴾
ayahs.meaning: The servant announced their parting and promised to explain the confusing events.

options: Copy an action from the sacred story.
Seek immediate help from a trusted adult and keep safe.
Assume harm must be permitted for a hidden reason.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-KAHF • 18:71–78  |  FOCUS: 18:71, 18:74, 18:77, 18:78  |  TRAIT: Patience • Concern for others • Asking for help
missions.aim: Know that parts of sacred history can be difficult and that children must never copy harmful acts.
missions.tafsir: The account describes three events that Musa (AS) questioned: damage to a boat, the death of a boy and the repair of a wall in a town where hospitality was refused. Musa’s concern arises from the ordinary moral seriousness of these actions, and the story does not ask believers to imitate them. It is essential to explain that the servant’s actions were connected to special knowledge and instruction from Allah, as made explicit when he says he did not act on his own initiative (18:82). Ordinary people cannot claim unseen information to justify harming a person or damaging property. Classical Tafsir treats these events as exceptional to this account. For younger children, narrate that three events confused Musa, without depicting the boy’s death or inviting role-play. The proper everyday response to harm is to protect others and seek trusted adult or emergency help.
missions.story: Akhlaq listened quietly while Sheikh Uncle summarized Musa’s difficult journey. At one point he looked puzzled. “If something seems wrong,” he asked, “should I stay silent?” Sheikh Uncle answered gently, “No. Never ignore someone in danger. This was a special event in revelation, and it is not a rule for our choices.” Imaan pointed to the class safety poster: ask questions, tell a trusted adult, and protect people. They then chose a different puzzle to practice patient thinking: a classroom shelf had been moved, and the children did not yet know why. When the teacher explained that a wheelchair needed more space, they understood how an ordinary harmless change may have a good reason. The Qur’anic story remained separate from their safe classroom example.
missions.question: A child sees someone being hurt. What should the child do?
missions.feedback: No one may use this account as permission for harm; child safety comes first.
missions.action: Learn where to find a trusted adult at school or home if someone is unsafe.
missions.reflection: Why is asking for help a sign of wisdom?
missions.careNote: Critical: no violence animation, reenactment, harm simulation or child-blaming; special revelation does not authorize present-day wrongdoing.
missions.next: The explanations of those events follow, including a reminder that Allah knows what we cannot.
missions.sourcePath: Qur’an 18:71–78 • al-Tabari / Ibn Kathir / al-Munir • https://quran.com/18/71

missions.title: The Explanation and the Trust

ayahs.arabic: أَمَّا ٱلسَّفِينَةُ فَكَانَتْ لِمَسَـٰكِينَ يَعْمَلُونَ فِى ٱلْبَحْرِ فَأَرَدتُّ أَنْ أَعِيبَهَا وَكَانَ وَرَآءَهُم مَّلِكٌ يَأْخُذُ كُلَّ سَفِينَةٍ غَصْبًا  ﴿79﴾
ayahs.meaning: The boat belonged to poor sea workers; a ruler was seizing sound boats, so it was damaged to protect it.

ayahs.arabic: وَأَمَّا ٱلْغُلَـٰمُ فَكَانَ أَبَوَاهُ مُؤْمِنَيْنِ فَخَشِينَآ أَن يُرْهِقَهُمَا طُغْيَـٰنًا وَكُفْرًا  ﴿80﴾
ayahs.meaning: The passage explains the servant’s specially revealed concern regarding the boy’s believing parents.

ayahs.arabic: فَأَرَدْنَآ أَن يُبْدِلَهُمَا رَبُّهُمَا خَيْرًا مِّنْهُ زَكَوٰةً وَأَقْرَبَ رُحْمًا  ﴿81﴾
ayahs.meaning: Allah intended something better for the parents; this is exceptional divine knowledge, not a human permission.

ayahs.arabic: وَأَمَّا ٱلْجِدَارُ فَكَانَ لِغُلَـٰمَيْنِ يَتِيمَيْنِ فِى ٱلْمَدِينَةِ وَكَانَ تَحْتَهُۥ كَنزٌ لَّهُمَا وَكَانَ أَبُوهُمَا صَـٰلِحًا فَأَرَادَ رَبُّكَ أَن يَبْلُغَآ أَشُدَّهُمَا وَيَسْتَخْرِجَا كَنزَهُمَا رَحْمَةً مِّن رَّبِّكَ ۚ وَمَا فَعَلْتُهُۥ عَنْ أَمْرِى ۚ ذَٰلِكَ تَأْوِيلُ مَا لَمْ تَسْطِع عَّلَيْهِ صَبْرًا  ﴿82﴾
ayahs.meaning: The wall protected the treasure of two orphans; the servant says he did not act by his own initiative.

options: Damage it secretly because you think you know best.
Ask the responsible adult and help in a lawful, safe way.
Tell everyone the owner deserves trouble.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-KAHF • 18:79–82  |  FOCUS: 18:79, 18:80, 18:81, 18:82  |  TRAIT: Justice • Trust • Humility about unseen
missions.aim: Learn that the events had explanations given by revelation and that people must still obey ordinary moral rules.
missions.tafsir: The servant explains the boat belonged to poor people working at sea; a ruler was taking sound ships, so damage was connected to its protection. He also explains the deeply difficult incident concerning the boy, and the wall safeguarding a treasure belonging to two orphans whose father was righteous. He concludes that he did not act on his own authority. Scholars stress the distinction between special divine knowledge in this exceptional narrative and the normal requirements of the Shari‘ah. No child or adult today may damage a boat or harm another person because they think they know an unseen outcome. For children, the positive applications should emphasize protecting the rights of vulnerable people, not judging tragedies or pretending to know Allah’s hidden plans. The full sacred text remains available with content warnings and adult support.
missions.story: A heavy rainstorm loosened the lid on Amanpur’s neighbourhood book-exchange box. Mohsin wanted to close it with his own padlock, but Imaan suggested asking the caretaker first. They learned that a neighbour had been repairing the hinges and would reopen the box safely. The children helped protect the donated books without making assumptions or taking someone else’s property. Sheikh Uncle later explained that the final verses of Musa’s (AS) journey revealed reasons unknown at the time, but this special story must never become an excuse for ordinary people to do harm. Akhlaq remembered the lesson as a combination of two things: we do not know everything, and we must still behave justly.
missions.question: You suspect someone’s property needs protection. What is the wisest action?
missions.feedback: Protecting others requires permission, wisdom and ordinary moral responsibility.
missions.action: Ask permission before helping to move or repair something that belongs to someone else.
missions.reflection: How can I respect the limits of my knowledge while still doing right?
missions.vocabulary: ʿAdl — justice; ʿIlm al-ghayb — knowledge of the unseen
missions.careNote: Full Arabic verses 18:80–81 are retained, with parent/teacher handling. No “hidden wisdom” excuse for abuse or unsafe events.
missions.next: Next we meet Dhul-Qarnayn, a leader tested by the power he possessed.

missions.title: Strength with Justice

ayahs.arabic: وَيَسْـَٔلُونَكَ عَن ذِى ٱلْقَرْنَيْنِ ۖ قُلْ سَأَتْلُوا۟ عَلَيْكُم مِّنْهُ ذِكْرًا  ﴿83﴾
ayahs.meaning: The Prophet ﷺ is asked about Dhul-Qarnayn, and Allah gives an account of him.

ayahs.arabic: إِنَّا مَكَّنَّا لَهُۥ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ وَءَاتَيْنَـٰهُ مِن كُلِّ شَىْءٍ سَبَبًا  ﴿84﴾
ayahs.meaning: Allah established him and granted him means for his undertakings.

ayahs.arabic: قَالَ أَمَّا مَن ظَلَمَ فَسَوْفَ نُعَذِّبُهُۥ ثُمَّ يُرَدُّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّهِۦ فَيُعَذِّبُهُۥ عَذَابًا نُّكْرًا  ﴿87﴾
ayahs.meaning: The leader explained that wrongdoing would face just consequences.

ayahs.arabic: وَأَمَّا مَنْ ءَامَنَ وَعَمِلَ صَـٰلِحًا فَلَهُۥ جَزَآءً ٱلْحُسْنَىٰ ۖ وَسَنَقُولُ لَهُۥ مِنْ أَمْرِنَا يُسْرًا  ﴿88﴾
ayahs.meaning: Belief and righteous deeds would receive good treatment and ease.

options: Always favour his closest friends.
Give fair opportunities and ask an adult for help in disputes.
Threaten anyone who disagrees.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-KAHF • 18:83–88  |  FOCUS: 18:83, 18:84, 18:87, 18:88  |  TRAIT: Leadership • Fairness • Responsibility
missions.aim: Understand that power is an Amanah to be used justly, not to frighten weaker people.
missions.tafsir: Dhul-Qarnayn is introduced as a ruler to whom Allah gave means and opportunities. He travelled widely, and the verses relate his commitment to just treatment: wrongdoing has consequences, while those who believe and act rightly are promised good. Classical Tafsir discusses his history and identity, but the Qur’an does not require children to identify him confidently with a named ancient emperor. The reliable lesson is justice, accountability and stewardship. A child leader in the classroom must not imitate royal punishment or issue threats. A safe, age-appropriate application is treating classmates fairly, hearing all sides and seeking an adult to resolve serious disputes. Our animation can show routes, landmarks and acts of help without portraying Dhul-Qarnayn as an invented historical portrait.
missions.story: At school, Akhlaq was selected to coordinate a football team. Two players were his closest friends, and he almost gave them every turn. Imaan asked how the quieter children would feel. Akhlaq made a turn-taking chart and explained it to the team. When a disagreement arose, he listened to both players before asking the teacher to help settle it. Sheikh Uncle later told them that Dhul-Qarnayn was entrusted with great means and was expected to act justly. “Even small leadership is a trust,” he said. Akhlaq looked at the chart again. Being the leader had not made him more important than anyone else; it had given him a responsibility to be fair.
missions.question: As team leader, how should Akhlaq choose players?
missions.feedback: Leadership is service and fair responsibility, not personal privilege.
missions.action: When sharing a game or activity today, give everyone a fair turn.
missions.careNote: Historical identity debated: no definitive Alexander portrayal or punishment role-play.
missions.next: The account continues as the leader meets other communities.
missions.sourcePath: Qur’an 18:83–88 • al-Tabari / Ibn Kathir / al-Munir • https://quran.com/18/83

missions.title: Listening Across Different Lands

ayahs.arabic: ثُمَّ أَتْبَعَ سَبَبًا  ﴿89﴾
ayahs.meaning: He followed another route.

ayahs.arabic: حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَا بَلَغَ مَطْلِعَ ٱلشَّمْسِ وَجَدَهَا تَطْلُعُ عَلَىٰ قَوْمٍ لَّمْ نَجْعَل لَّهُم مِّن دُونِهَا سِتْرًا  ﴿90﴾
ayahs.meaning: The account describes what Dhul-Qarnayn encountered toward the rising of the sun.

ayahs.arabic: ثُمَّ أَتْبَعَ سَبَبًا  ﴿92﴾
ayahs.meaning: He followed another route.

ayahs.arabic: حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَا بَلَغَ بَيْنَ ٱلسَّدَّيْنِ وَجَدَ مِن دُونِهِمَا قَوْمًا لَّا يَكَادُونَ يَفْقَهُونَ قَوْلًا  ﴿93﴾
ayahs.meaning: He reached between two barriers and found a people who could scarcely understand speech.

options: Mock the unfamiliar words.
Listen patiently and ask a teacher to help communicate.
Assume the child cannot learn.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-KAHF • 18:89–93  |  FOCUS: 18:89, 18:90, 18:92, 18:93  |  TRAIT: Empathy • Observation • Communication
missions.aim: Practise listening when people live differently or speak in unfamiliar ways.
missions.tafsir: Dhul-Qarnayn continues his journeys and reaches communities in differing places and circumstances. The passage describes what he observed on his route and then a people whose speech was difficult for him or his party to understand. Classical Tafsir notes the travel narrative but does not provide a universally agreed modern map. We should not teach that the sun literally enters a spring or use the language of sunrise and sunset as a science error; it is how a traveller describes what appears to the eye. The ethical application for children is patient listening and respect across language and cultural differences. Communication difficulties do not make a community less intelligent or less worthy. A good learner asks, observes carefully, and seeks suitable translation or adult support.
missions.story: A new family arrived in Amanpur, and their child spoke a different home language. Akhlaq initially repeated a word he could not understand and made some classmates laugh. Imaan asked him to stop. They invited the child to show them the meaning through pictures and gestures. The teacher helped everyone learn how to pronounce the child’s name. Later, Sheikh Uncle described how Dhul-Qarnayn encountered people whose words were difficult to understand. “Different speech is not a reason for mockery,” he said. The next day Akhlaq welcomed the new classmate with a smile and a carefully practised greeting. The two children began building a model bridge together, finding ways to communicate beyond words.
missions.question: You cannot understand a new classmate’s language. What should you do?
missions.feedback: Communication takes patience, dignity and mutual effort.
missions.action: Learn to pronounce one unfamiliar name respectfully and use it correctly.
missions.reflection: How can we welcome someone whose language is new to us?
missions.vocabulary: Taʿāruf — getting to know one another; Riḥlah — journey
missions.careNote: No fixed historical map, identity claims or simplistic labels about people groups; distinguish visual appearance from astronomy.
missions.next: Now a community asks for protection and Dhul-Qarnayn organizes a collective effort.
missions.sourcePath: Qur’an 18:89–93 • al-Tabari / Ibn Kathir / al-Munir • https://quran.com/18/89

missions.title: The Barrier Built Together

ayahs.arabic: قَالُوا۟ يَـٰذَا ٱلْقَرْنَيْنِ إِنَّ يَأْجُوجَ وَمَأْجُوجَ مُفْسِدُونَ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ فَهَلْ نَجْعَلُ لَكَ خَرْجًا عَلَىٰٓ أَن تَجْعَلَ بَيْنَنَا وَبَيْنَهُمْ سَدًّا  ﴿94﴾
ayahs.meaning: The people asked for a barrier against Ya’juj and Ma’juj, who caused corruption.

ayahs.arabic: قَالَ مَا مَكَّنِّى فِيهِ رَبِّى خَيْرٌ فَأَعِينُونِى بِقُوَّةٍ أَجْعَلْ بَيْنَكُمْ وَبَيْنَهُمْ رَدْمًا  ﴿95﴾
ayahs.meaning: He declined to make gain the centre of the effort and requested the people’s physical help.

ayahs.arabic: ءَاتُونِى زُبَرَ ٱلْحَدِيدِ ۖ حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَا سَاوَىٰ بَيْنَ ٱلصَّدَفَيْنِ قَالَ ٱنفُخُوا۟ ۖ حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَا جَعَلَهُۥ نَارًا قَالَ ءَاتُونِىٓ أُفْرِغْ عَلَيْهِ قِطْرًا  ﴿96﴾
ayahs.meaning: The Qur’an describes constructing the barrier with iron and molten copper.

ayahs.arabic: فَمَا ٱسْطَـٰعُوٓا۟ أَن يَظْهَرُوهُ وَمَا ٱسْتَطَـٰعُوا۟ لَهُۥ نَقْبًا  ﴿97﴾
ayahs.meaning: The barrier could neither be scaled nor penetrated by the aggressors at that time.

ayahs.arabic: قَالَ هَـٰذَا رَحْمَةٌ مِّن رَّبِّى ۖ فَإِذَا جَآءَ وَعْدُ رَبِّى جَعَلَهُۥ دَكَّآءَ ۖ وَكَانَ وَعْدُ رَبِّى حَقًّا  ﴿98﴾
ayahs.meaning: Dhul-Qarnayn called the barrier a mercy from Allah and said Allah’s promise would come true.

options: Try dangerous repairs without adult supervision.
Report the problem and support trained adults with safe teamwork.
Ignore it because someone else will manage.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-KAHF • 18:94–98  |  FOCUS: 18:94, 18:95, 18:96, 18:97, 18:98  |  TRAIT: Teamwork • Protection • Gratitude
missions.aim: Learn how a leader and community can work together to protect others and thank Allah for success.
missions.tafsir: A community explains that Ya’juj and Ma’juj cause corruption and asks Dhul-Qarnayn to build a protective barrier. Instead of treating the task as an opportunity for mere personal gain, he asks the community to support the work with effort. The Qur’an describes construction using iron and molten copper, followed by an acknowledgement that the result is a mercy from Allah and will not last beyond His appointed decree. Classical Tafsir emphasizes Allah’s granting of means, the ruler’s just action and the reality of future events. Children must not be asked to imitate the dangerous work with real heat, metal or tools. The suitable modern application is planning a safe community service project and sharing the credit. Do not invent the barrier’s exact historical location or depict Ya’juj and Ma’juj as identifiable modern peoples.
missions.story: The community library’s front step became slippery after rain. Imaan noticed that smaller children had trouble climbing it. Akhlaq wanted to repair it by himself, but Salaam explained that building work required trained adults. The children gathered suggestions, drew a safe access plan and asked the school administration for help. A professional repaired the step while the children organized a temporary safe route. Sheikh Uncle told them how Dhul-Qarnayn joined leadership with collective effort and acknowledged Allah’s mercy after the great barrier was built. When the new step was opened, Akhlaq thanked the workers and classmates rather than claiming the project as his own. Teamwork, he found, could protect people without making any one person the hero.
missions.question: What is the best way to improve an unsafe school entrance?
missions.feedback: Good leadership invites help, protects people and thanks Allah.
missions.action: Help identify one simple community need and share a safe suggestion with an adult.
missions.reflection: Who deserves thanks when a team accomplishes something good?
missions.careNote: No dangerous DIY metallurgy, demonizing modern ethnic groups, or falsely identifying the precise barrier.
missions.next: The surah ends by reminding us what real success means beyond any monument.
missions.sourcePath: Qur’an 18:94–98 • al-Tabari / Ibn Kathir / al-Munir • https://quran.com/18/94

missions.title: A Good Ending: Faith and Sincere Deeds

ayahs.arabic: وَتَرَكْنَا بَعْضَهُمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ يَمُوجُ فِى بَعْضٍ ۖ وَنُفِخَ فِى ٱلصُّورِ فَجَمَعْنَـٰهُمْ جَمْعًا  ﴿99﴾
ayahs.meaning: The passage points forward to the final gathering and the blowing of the Trumpet.

ayahs.arabic: قُلْ هَلْ نُنَبِّئُكُم بِٱلْأَخْسَرِينَ أَعْمَـٰلًا  ﴿103﴾
ayahs.meaning: The Prophet ﷺ is told to ask whether people should be informed about those most unsuccessful in deeds.

ayahs.arabic: ٱلَّذِينَ ضَلَّ سَعْيُهُمْ فِى ٱلْحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا وَهُمْ يَحْسَبُونَ أَنَّهُمْ يُحْسِنُونَ صُنْعًا  ﴿104﴾
ayahs.meaning: Some people’s efforts are lost while they mistakenly imagine themselves doing well.

ayahs.arabic: أُو۟لَـٰٓئِكَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ بِـَٔايَـٰتِ رَبِّهِمْ وَلِقَآئِهِۦ فَحَبِطَتْ أَعْمَـٰلُهُمْ فَلَا نُقِيمُ لَهُمْ يَوْمَ ٱلْقِيَـٰمَةِ وَزْنًا  ﴿105﴾
ayahs.meaning: Those who deny their Lord’s signs and the meeting with Him lose their deeds.

ayahs.arabic: إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ وَعَمِلُوا۟ ٱلصَّـٰلِحَـٰتِ كَانَتْ لَهُمْ جَنَّـٰتُ ٱلْفِرْدَوْسِ نُزُلًا  ﴿107﴾
ayahs.meaning: Believers who act righteously are promised the gardens of Paradise.

ayahs.arabic: قُلْ إِنَّمَآ أَنَا۠ بَشَرٌ مِّثْلُكُمْ يُوحَىٰٓ إِلَىَّ أَنَّمَآ إِلَـٰهُكُمْ إِلَـٰهٌ وَٰحِدٌ ۖ فَمَن كَانَ يَرْجُوا۟ لِقَآءَ رَبِّهِۦ فَلْيَعْمَلْ عَمَلًا صَـٰلِحًا وَلَا يُشْرِكْ بِعِبَادَةِ رَبِّهِۦٓ أَحَدًۢا  ﴿110﴾
ayahs.meaning: The Messenger ﷺ receives revelation that Allah is One; whoever hopes to meet Him should do good and worship Him alone.

options: Stop helping unless everyone praises you.
Keep doing good for Allah’s sake.
Tell everyone you are more righteous.
missions.anchor: SURAH AL-KAHF • 18:99–110  |  FOCUS: 18:99, 18:103, 18:104, 18:105, 18:107, 18:110  |  TRAIT: Sincerity • Sound belief • Righteous action
missions.aim: Remember that faith in Allah, sincere worship and good deeds matter more than appearance or recognition.
missions.tafsir: The closing passage speaks about the Last Day, accountability, deeds that are lost because of rejection of Allah’s guidance, and the reward prepared for believers who do good. Verse 110 ends the surah with a concise message: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is a human messenger who receives revelation that your God is One; whoever hopes to meet their Lord must do righteous deeds and not associate anyone in worship with Him. Classical commentators connect right belief with sincere good action, rejecting both empty boasting and worship directed to others. For children, the message is hopeful and concrete: learn Tawhid, practise kindness, make sincere efforts and ask Allah for forgiveness after mistakes. Avoid turning the theological warnings into a game that judges individual children’s salvation or ranks their Iman.
missions.story: The Amanpur school held a small celebration for students who had helped the community. Imaan and Akhlaq applauded the gardeners, readers, helpers and cleaners. Later Akhlaq asked Sheikh Uncle whether a good deed still mattered when nobody gave a certificate. Sheikh Uncle recited the final message of Surah Al-Kahf: worship Allah alone and do righteous deeds sincerely. “A certificate can encourage us,” he said, “but our purpose is greater than being seen.” Imaan remembered the young believers, the two gardens, Musa’s journey and Dhul-Qarnayn’s teamwork. Each account had taught them to choose Allah’s guidance over pride. They decided that their next kindness project should begin quietly, with a sincere intention and one useful action.
missions.question: Nobody notices your helpful act. What should you do?
missions.feedback: Sincere worship and righteous actions do not depend on public rewards.
missions.action: Do one useful act quietly today and make a sincere intention for Allah.
missions.reflection: Which story from Al-Kahf most changed how I want to behave?
missions.vocabulary: Ikhlāṣ — sincerity; Tawḥīd — worshipping Allah alone
missions.careNote: Do not judge individual children’s ultimate reward. Explain the Hereafter with hope, respect and qualified guidance.
